title: Eating with Others Better for Blood Sugar — Study
paragraphs: It's not uncommon to eat meals alone. Sometimes it's because no one else is around when you want to eat. Sometimes you just don't want company.
However, research has found that dining alone might be worse for your blood sugar.
A study published in Science Advances looked at what happened to 108 participants' blood sugar after eating around 100 grams of white bread, both alone and with someone they were close with.
When people ate bread with a close companion, they had lower blood sugar spikes than when they ate alone, and their glucose levels went back to normal more quickly.

Spikes in blood sugar after eating aren't unusual. They happen because when we eat carbohydrates, our bodies break them down into glucose — or sugar — which goes into our bloodstream. The body then uses the hormone insulin to push that glucose into cells where it will be used as energy.

However, regularly having high blood sugar spikes may negatively affect your long-term health and increase your risk of things like heart disease. These spikes can also affect your energy, mood and sleep.
The bread experiment was one of several the researchers used to look at "social physiology," or the idea that being with others affects how well our bodies work.

Another experiment found that people had better temperature regulation in the cold when they were with a partner. The effect was stronger when they had physical contact, but there were benefits even when they weren't touching.
In another test, babies showed a lower physical stress response to a scary noise if their mothers were with them.
The researchers also ran a test in which participants were given mild electric shocks, and their physical stress responses were lower when they were with someone else.
According to the researchers, this all shows that relationships don't just support us emotionally — they may also help regulate our body's basic systems.
